title: Radioactive decay
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for IB Diploma Physics (status of the source: ai-reviewed-reverified-gate-verified-2026-09-29-awaiting-human-signoff). Terms and clues: E.3#c15 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; E.3.9#xt1 term and clue written for the game; E.3.11#xt1 term and clue written for the game; E.3.10#xt1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: E.3#q10, E.3#q11, E.3#q13, E.3#q14, E.3#q18, E.3#q20, E.3#q22, E.3#q36, E.3#q12, E.3#q37, E.3#q15, E.3#q19, E.3#q23, E.3#q24, E.3#q25, E.3#q27, E.3#q28, E.3#q29.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Gamma (γ) radiation
items.clue: A high-energy photon emitted when a nucleus drops to a lower energy state.

items.label: Antineutrino
items.clue: Uncharged and almost massless; emitted together with the electron in β⁻ decay.

items.label: Half-life
items.clue: The time taken for the activity of a sample to fall to 50% of its initial value.

items.label: Alpha particle
items.clue: A helium nucleus: the most ionizing but least penetrating emission, stopped by paper.

questions.stem: A nucleus X undergoes α decay. The daughter nucleus then undergoes two β⁻ decays in succession. How does the final nucleus compare with X?

options.text: It is an isotope of X whose nucleus has six fewer neutrons than X.
It is another element, with two fewer protons and two fewer neutrons.
It is another element, with four fewer protons and as many neutrons as X.
It is an isotope of X whose nucleus has four fewer neutrons than X.

questions.explanation: α decay removes 2 protons and 2 neutrons; each β⁻ decay turns a neutron into a proton. Overall Z is unchanged (−2 + 1 + 1) and N falls by 2 + 1 + 1 = 4, so the result is an isotope of X with a nucleon number 4 less.

questions.stem: Which of these radioactive decay equations is correct?

options.text: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e + ⁰₀ν
¹⁸₉F → ¹⁸₁₀Ne + ⁰₊₁e + ⁰₀ν
²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂α
¹³⁷ᵐ₅₆Ba → ¹³⁷₅₅Cs + γ

questions.explanation: Nucleon number: 226 = 222 + 4. Charge: 88 = 86 + 2. An α particle is a helium-4 nucleus, so radium (Z = 88) becomes radon (Z = 86).

questions.stem: An electron antineutrino, ν̄, is emitted in every β⁻ decay. Which statement about the antineutrino is correct?

options.text: It is a neutron that leaves the nucleus together with the β⁻ particle.
It is uncharged, has a very small mass and very rarely interacts with matter.
It is positively charged, balancing the negative charge of the β⁻ particle.
It is a high-energy photon, emitted as the new nucleus loses energy.

questions.explanation: Antineutrinos, like neutrinos, have zero charge and a mass far smaller than the electron's, and they interact so rarely that almost all of them pass straight through the Earth.

questions.stem: Technetium-99m emits γ rays only and has a half-life of 6.0 h. It is injected into patients so that the organs that take it up can be imaged by a γ camera outside the body. Which statement is a correct reason for choosing technetium-99m?

options.text: Its γ rays are strongly ionizing, so they give a strong signal at the camera.
Its half-life is short because so little is injected, and a small sample halves quickly.
Its γ rays make the organ's own tissue radioactive, so that the organ shows up.
Its γ rays are weakly ionizing and most pass out of the body to the camera.

questions.explanation: γ rays are the most penetrating and least ionizing radiation, so most pass out of the body to the camera and relatively little energy is deposited in the patient. The short half-life then limits the dose after the scan.

questions.stem: Cobalt-60 has a half-life of 5.3 years and decays into nickel-60, a stable solid. A sample contains a large number of cobalt-60 nuclei. Which statement about the sample is correct?

options.text: After 5.3 years, about half of the cobalt-60 nuclei present now will remain.
After 10.6 years, all of the cobalt-60 nuclei will have decayed.
After 5.3 years, the sample's mass will be about half of its mass now.
A sample twice as large would take 10.6 years to fall to half.

questions.explanation: Half-life is the time for the number of undecayed nuclei to halve. With a large number of nuclei, the fraction that decays in 5.3 years is very close to one half.

questions.stem: A hospital prepares a dose of technetium-99m (half-life 6.0 h) that has an activity of 800 MBq at 08:00. What will its activity be at 14:00 the next day?

options.text: 0 MBq
160 MBq
25 MBq
12.5 MBq

questions.explanation: From 08:00 to 14:00 the next day is 30 h, which is five half-lives: 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 → 50 → 25 MBq.

questions.stem: A detector placed near a source of half-life 2.0 days records 250 counts min⁻¹. With the source removed, it records a background of 50 counts min⁻¹. What will the detector record with the source in the same place 6.0 days later?

options.text: 75 counts min⁻¹
31 counts min⁻¹
25 counts min⁻¹
50 counts min⁻¹

questions.explanation: Only the source's contribution halves. Corrected rate now: 250 − 50 = 200 counts min⁻¹. After 3 half-lives: 200/8 = 25 counts min⁻¹. The detector still records the background too: 25 + 50 = 75 counts min⁻¹.

questions.stem: A nucleus emits a β⁺ particle, and the daughter nucleus then emits a γ photon. How do the proton number Z and neutron number N of the final nucleus compare with those of the original nucleus?

options.text: Z is one more, and N is one less.
Z is one less; N is unchanged.
Z is one less and N is one more.
Neither Z nor N has changed.

questions.explanation: In β⁺ decay a proton in the nucleus changes into a neutron, emitting a positron and a neutrino: Z falls by one and N rises by one (A unchanged). γ emission carries away energy only, leaving Z and N as they are.

questions.stem: The four decays below involve nuclides used in medicine and industry. Which decay equation is correct?

options.text: ¹³¹₅₃I → ¹³¹₅₄Xe + ⁰₋₁e + ⁰₀ν̄
²⁴¹₉₅Am → ²³⁷₉₃Np + ⁴₂α + ⁰₀ν
¹⁸₉F → ¹⁸₈O + ⁰₊₁e + ⁰₀ν̄
⁹⁰₃₈Sr → ⁸⁹₃₉Y + ⁰₋₁e + ⁰₀ν̄

questions.explanation: Nucleon number: 131 = 131 + 0 + 0. Charge: 53 = 54 + (−1) + 0. In β⁻ decay a neutron becomes a proton, and an electron and an electron antineutrino are emitted.

questions.stem: Fluorine-18, used in PET scanning, decays by β⁺ emission: ¹⁸₉F → ¹⁸₈O + e⁺ + X. What is the particle X?

options.text: an antineutrino, ν̄, from the nucleus
a neutron, n, from the nucleus
a γ photon emitted by the nucleus
a neutrino, ν, from the nucleus

questions.explanation: β⁺ decay is p → n + e⁺ + ν: the positron is accompanied by a neutrino. The neutrino has zero charge and nucleon number zero, so both sides of the equation balance (charge 9 = 8 + 1 + 0; nucleon number 18 = 18 + 0 + 0).

questions.stem: A small amount of sodium-24 (half-life 15 h), which emits β⁻ particles and γ rays, is added to water flowing in a pipe buried 1 m underground. A detector moved along the surface above the pipe records a much higher count rate above one point. Which statement explains this reading?

options.text: β⁻ particles from the leaked tracer have the energy to cross a metre of soil.
The tracer decays faster once it is out of the pipe, so it emits more there.
γ rays from the tracer that has leaked into the soil pass up through the ground.
The water's γ rays make the soil around the leak radioactive, and this is detected.

questions.stem: To determine the half-life of a nuclide, a student measures the count rate from a sample and the background count rate. After subtracting the background, the count rate falls from 640 counts s⁻¹ at t = 0 to 80 counts s⁻¹ at t = 120 min. What is the half-life of the nuclide?

options.text: 69 min
15 min
30 min
40 min

questions.explanation: 640 → 320 → 160 → 80 counts s⁻¹ is three halvings, so 120 min is three half-lives and T½ = 40 min.

questions.stem: In a helium-4 nucleus the two protons are about 2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m apart. At this separation the electric repulsion between them is about 58 N, an enormous force on particles of mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. Yet helium-4 nuclei are stable. What does this evidence show?

options.text: Gravitational attraction between protons this close together balances the repulsion.
The neutrons attract the protons, but the two protons exert no attraction on each other.
An attraction stronger than the electric repulsion must act between nucleons.
A long-range attraction acts, which also binds the nuclei of neighbouring atoms together.

questions.stem: The stable isotopes of carbon are ¹²₆C and ¹³₆C. Carbon-14 (¹⁴₆C) is radioactive. Which decay does carbon-14 undergo, and why?

options.text: β⁺ decay, as this turns one of its surplus neutrons into a proton
β⁻ decay, as a neutron changes into a proton and lowers its N/Z ratio
α decay, as the α particle carries two of its surplus neutrons away with it
γ emission, which lets it shed its surplus neutrons as energy

questions.explanation: With 8 neutrons and 6 protons (N/Z = 1.33), carbon-14 is neutron-rich compared with the stable isotopes (N/Z = 1.00 and 1.17). β⁻ decay turns a neutron into a proton, giving ¹⁴₇N (N/Z = 1), which is stable.

questions.stem: For nuclides with nucleon number A above about 60, the binding energy per nucleon changes very little, staying between about 7.6 MeV and 8.8 MeV. What does this suggest about the strong nuclear force?

options.text: Each nucleon attracts every other nucleon in the nucleus, as the force has a long range.
It gives every nucleus with A above 60 about the same total binding energy.
It is so strong that the repulsion between protons has no effect in large nuclei.
Each nucleon is attracted only by its nearest neighbours, as the force has a very short range.

questions.stem: In the β⁻ decay of a particular nuclide, the emitted electrons have a continuous range of kinetic energies, from almost zero up to a maximum value. Which statement correctly explains this?

options.text: The energy released is shared in varying proportions between the electron and an antineutrino.
Electrons lose different amounts of energy in collisions with atoms before they leave the source.
The electrons come from different shells of the atom, which have different binding energies.
The daughter nucleus can be left with any energy, as nuclear energy levels are continuous.

questions.stem: The activity per gram of carbon in a sample of bone is 23% of that in living tissue. Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5730 years. Assuming the proportion of carbon-14 in living tissue has not changed, what is the age of the bone?
questions.explanation: With λ = ln 2/5730 y = 1.21 × 10⁻⁴ y⁻¹, 0.23 = e^(−λt) gives t = ln(1/0.23)/λ = 1.2 × 10⁴ years: between two and three half-lives, as expected for a fall to 23%.

questions.stem: A nuclide has a decay constant λ = 0.10 s⁻¹. What is the probability that a particular undecayed nucleus of this nuclide decays within the next 5.0 s?
questions.explanation: The probability of surviving 5.0 s is e^(−λt) = e^(−0.50) = 0.61, so the probability of decaying is 1 − 0.61 = 0.39. Here λt = 0.50 is not small, so λt is not a good approximation.
